Deep Neck Infections

trismus with a deviated uvula needs no imaging · deep neck spaces by age · epiglottitis and Ludwig angina: airway firstHow old is the child, and is it trismus, pain on neck extension, or tripoding with stridor?

Source vignette Pt – boy of 14 whose throat pain on one side has grown worse over a week; he cannot open his jaw fully, his speech sounds muffled and the uvula leans to the left · Q – the likeliest diagnosis; choices covered peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess and infectious mononucleosis

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Days of worsening one-sided throat pain, trismus, muffled speech and a uvula pushed away from a discrete tonsillar bulge in an adolescent is a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). It is a clinical diagnosis: no imaging unless spread beyond the tonsil is suspected.
  • Drain it, by needle aspiration or incision and drainage, and give antibiotics that cover aerobes and anaerobes; most patients go home.
  • Under age 5, often after a cold, fever, drooling and a neck that will not extend: retropharyngeal abscess, imaged by CT neck with contrast. A tooth infection with a board-hard floor of the mouth: Ludwig angina. In both, and in a tripoding child, the airway comes first.
What it is

Pus or spreading infection in the potential spaces of the neck. The Step 2 anchor is peritonsillar abscess, a collection between the tonsil and the superior pharyngeal constrictor and the most common deep neck infection.

Bug

Peritonsillar abscess: polymicrobial; aerobes led by streptococci (group A first) and staphylococci, with oral anaerobes such as Fusobacterium and Bacteroides.

Retropharyngeal abscess: group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus and Bacteroides.

Ludwig angina: mixed oral aerobes and anaerobes from a lower tooth.

Spread

Peritonsillar: adolescents and young adults; one side, from tonsillar infection.

Retropharyngeal: 6 months to 6 years, usually after an upper respiratory infection seeds the retropharyngeal nodes; those nodes regress by about age 5, so an older child or adult needs another route, such as a swallowed foreign body or instrumentation.

Ludwig angina: usually an infected lower molar; poor dental hygiene, an extraction or jaw trauma may contribute.

Chain

Tonsillar infection

pus collects between the tonsil and the superior constrictor

a discrete one-sided bulge pushes the soft palate and uvula across

jaw muscle spasm (trismus) and a muffled voice

untreated, spread to the parapharyngeal space, the mediastinum or the carotid sheath, or rupture with aspiration

Insights

Pronounced trismus and a shifted uvula point to a discrete abscess; cellulitis swells the same area without the bulge, and the exam alone separates them poorly, so the needle decides.

Age sorts the spaces: the retropharyngeal nodes regress by about age 5, so a retropharyngeal abscess belongs to the toddler, and a teenager with a one-sided bulge has a peritonsillar one.

2Urgent risks
Urgent findings
FindingAction
Stridor or drooling with any deep neck infectionAirway first: secure it before imaging, antibiotics or drainage (route in step 7).
Tripoding, drooling and stridor in an unvaccinated child whose throat looks normalEpiglottitis: no tongue depressor; the airway is examined in the operating room.
Board-hard floor of the mouth and a tongue pushed up after a tooth infectionLudwig angina: it can block the airway within hours; secure it first.
Rigors, high fever and bacteremia, or bleeding from the throat, with a deep neck abscessMay mean carotid sheath involvement from the posterior parapharyngeal space: contrast CT neck now.
3Differential
The child or adolescent with a severe sore throat
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)Adolescent, days of worsening one-sided throat pain; trismus, a muffled voice, the uvula pushed to the other sideNeedle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics; no imaging.
Peritonsillar cellulitisThe same throat, swelling above the tonsil with no discrete bulge; a needle that finds no pus may mean cellulitisAntibiotics and fluids; it usually settles within 48 hours.
Retropharyngeal abscessUnder 5, often after an upper respiratory infection; will not extend the neck, drooling, a posterior pharyngeal wall bulging to one sideAirway first, then CT neck with contrast; incision and drainage with IV antibiotics.
Parapharyngeal abscessMimics a peritonsillar abscess, but swelling below the angle of the jaw, medial bulging of the pharyngeal wall, torticollisContrast CT neck, then IV antibiotics and drainage.
Ludwig angina (submandibular space infection)Lower tooth infection; board-hard floor of the mouth on both sides, the tongue pushed up, droolingAirway first; the diagnosis is usually clinical, CT only when it is not.
Unvaccinated, hours not days; tripoding, drooling with no barking cough, stridor, a normal-looking throatPerform laryngoscopy, usually flexible fiberoptic, in the operating room with airway rescue at hand; no tongue depressor.
Exudative tonsils on both sides with posterior cervical nodes and splenomegalyHeterophile antibody test; avoid amoxicillin and contact sports.
Swollen red tonsils, often with exudate, on both sides; nothing pushes the uvula asideRapid antigen test or culture; penicillin if positive.
Lemierre syndrome (septic jugular thrombophlebitis)May follow a throat infection: rigors, high fever, often bacteremia; a usually anaerobic infection of the internal jugular vein and the tissue around it, most often Fusobacterium necrophorum; it spreads most often to the lungs as nodular infiltrates that cavitateContrast CT neck and IV antibiotics that cover anaerobes.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
A rash after amoxicillin for a presumed strep throatMononucleosis; the rash is not a true allergyHeterophile antibody test; the rash fades once the antibiotic stops.
Retropharyngeal abscess in a teenager or adultA swallowed foreign body or instrumentation, since the nodes have regressedCT neck to define the extent.
Stridor that does not improve with racemic epinephrineNot croup: epiglottitis or a deep neck abscessSecure the airway, then CT neck with contrast.
Pause point
Teenager, one-sided sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula pushed across Offered as CT neck or lateral neck radiograph Can any image change a diagnosis the exam has already made? → Needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics; no imaging
A toddler, a week after a cold: fever, drooling, will not extend the neck, noisy breathing Offered as rapid strep test or oral antibiotics and home What comes before any test, and which study sees behind the pharynx? → Airway first, then CT neck with contrast; drainage and IV antibiotics
Tooth infection, board-hard floor of the mouth, tongue pushed up, drooling Offered as CT first or oral intubation What kills first, and which route works when the floor of the mouth is swollen? → Airway first, by awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation or tracheotomy; then drainage and IV antibiotics
5Diagnostic criteria
A clinical diagnosis: what makes it a peritonsillar abscess
ElementFinding
SymptomSevere sore throat, one-sided and worsening over days, with fever and ear pain
SignsTrismus, a muffled voice and a deviated uvula
Abscess, not cellulitisA discrete bulge, palate and uvula pushed across, pronounced trismus; pus on the needle
Imaging only whenThe exam is limited, the diagnosis is in doubt, or spread into the deep neck is suspected
6Severity
What makes it dangerous
FindingMeaning
Tonsils meeting in the midlineAirway threat: a reason to admit (step 8)
Swelling below the angle of the jaw or torticollisParapharyngeal spread
A retropharyngeal infection tracking toward the chestNecrotizing mediastinitis
Rigors, high fever, bacteremia, or bleeding from the throatThe carotid sheath: septic jugular thrombophlebitis (Lemierre syndrome) or arterial erosion; act as in step 2
7Treatment
1

AirwayAny deep neck infection with drooling, stridor or a hard floor of the mouth

Secure the airway before antibiotics, imaging or drainage. In Ludwig angina, awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation or a tracheotomy, because swelling defeats oral intubation.

2

Peritonsillar abscessClinical diagnosis

Drain it, by needle aspiration or incision and drainage, and give antibiotics covering group A Streptococcus and oral anaerobes (ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin); most patients go home. In practice: incision and drainage may carry a lower recurrence risk than aspiration alone (low-quality evidence), and corticosteroids may shorten symptoms.

3

Peritonsillar cellulitisNo pus on the needle, which may mean cellulitis

Antibiotics and fluids; it usually settles within 48 hours.

4

Retropharyngeal abscessChild with a collection behind the pharynx

Airway first, then incision and drainage with IV ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin. In practice: small abscesses in children are sometimes treated with IV antibiotics alone; surgery is kept for airway compromise, no response, a size over 3 cm, immune compromise or complications.

5

Parapharyngeal abscessCollection on contrast CT

IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone, and surgical drainage.

6

Ludwig anginaOnce the airway is safe

Incision and drainage and IV antibiotics covering oral aerobes and anaerobes.

7

Recurrent tonsillitisPeritonsillar abscess on a background of recurrent tonsillitis

Elective tonsillectomy 4 to 6 weeks later; tonsillectomy at presentation is rare, kept for a young or uncooperative child with other indications.

8Follow-up
After drainage
WhenDo
Dehydration, cannot drink, an airway concern, or failed outpatient careAdmit for IV antibiotics, fluids and airway monitoring.
Aspiration yields no pus but the picture persistsImage to confirm an abscess and ask otolaryngology about incision and drainage.
Group A Streptococcus grownPoststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (postinfectious glomerulonephritis) and rheumatic fever can follow.
Practice
  1. 14 yo M, week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left → Peritonsillar abscess → no imaging - needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics
  2. 14 yo M with a peritonsillar abscess, what must the antibiotics cover → Group A Streptococcus and respiratory anaerobes
  3. 4 yo M, fever and drooling with pain on neck extension and a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall → Retropharyngeal abscess → CT neck with contrast
  4. 5 yo M, unvaccinated, toxic and tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx → Epiglottitis → secure the airway in the operating room
  5. 17 yo F back from camp, bilateral exudative tonsils, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly → Infectious mononucleosis → heterophile antibody, avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
  6. 14 yo M whose drained abscess is followed by persistent fever, pleuritic chest pain and nodular lung opacities → Lemierre syndrome → contrast CT and anaerobic coverage
  7. 50 yo M with a dental infection, floor-of-mouth induration and tongue elevation → Ludwig angina → airway first
  8. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling where phlegmon versus abscess is uncertain → Intraoral ultrasound
  9. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling who develops new neck swelling and torticollis → Parapharyngeal extension → CT neck with contrast
  10. 14 yo M with a peritonsillar abscess drained today and years of recurrent tonsillitis; what prevents the next one → Tonsillectomy
  11. 6 yo F with bilateral exudates, no trismus, no uvular deviation, positive rapid strep → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → penicillin or amoxicillin
Airway before anything In Ludwig angina and epiglottitis, the airway is the emergency. Examination can precipitate obstruction, so do not depress the tongue or instrument the pharynx of a tripoding child outside the operating theatre. A peritonsillar abscess on a background of recurrent tonsillitis is an indication for elective tonsillectomy.
Pearls Peritonsillar abscess is diagnosed clinically; intraoral ultrasound helps when abscess versus cellulitis is uncertain and marks where to drain · Retropharyngeal abscess makes neck extension painful, so the child holds the neck still · Amoxicillin in undiagnosed mononucleosis brings a maculopapular rash that is not a true allergy · Lemierre syndrome is septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein after a throat infection, most often Fusobacterium necrophorum, and it spreads most often to the lungs as nodular infiltrates
Pairs with Respiratory Infection in a Child covers pharyngitis and its strep testing.
Noisy Breathing in a Child covers epiglottitis, croup and stridor.
Lymphadenopathy covers mononucleosis and neck nodes.
Ask: is anything one-sided?
Transferable rule When a diagnosis is clinical and the complication is airway compromise, imaging is almost always the wrong next step. It cannot change what is already known, and it costs time the airway may not have.
Sequencing trapImaging before drainage in a clinically obvious abscess.
Mirror twinRetropharyngeal abscess is the younger child's version, separated by extension versus trismus.
